summary: Discusses directions for the possible future evolution of the Internet architecture and suggests steps toward desired goals. It is an informational discussion document rather than a protocol specification, written when concerns about growth and addressing were mounting.

eli5.summary: Imagine a town planner writing down ideas for how the town should grow before it gets too crowded. This paper does that for the Internet and lists some steps to get there.

subtitle: Planning the Internet's evolution to handle massive growth and new applications.

tldr.problem: The Internet was growing exponentially and straining under its original architecture. Addressing would exhaust, routing tables would become unmanageable, and new capabilities like voice and video were needed but security remained ad-hoc.
tldr.mechanism: A group of Internet architects identified five key areas needing evolution: routing and addressing (aggregate networks), multi-protocol support (TCP/IP coexisting with OSI), security (perimeter-based and cryptographic), traffic control (for real-time data), and advanced applications (standardized formats and exchange methods).
tldr.outcome: The document laid groundwork for major changes including IPv6's larger address space, security architecture integration, and quality-of-service mechanisms that shaped the Internet's evolution over the following decade.

facts.label: Meeting timeline
facts.value: January 1991 (IAB/IESG initial discussion), June 1991 (three-day Architecture Retreat)

today: RFC 1287 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. Many of its recommendations shaped subsequent Internet standards: IPv6 expanded the address space to 128 bits, OSPF and BGP implemented address aggregation via autonomous systems, IPsec provided network-level security, and Integrated IS-IS supported both IP and OSI. Quality-of-service mechanisms like RSVP and later Differentiated Services brought traffic control to routers.

sections.title: The Internet's Growing Pains
sections.content:
By 1991, the Internet had grown from a small research network into a global infrastructure serving thousands of organizations. The original architecture, designed in the late 1970s, was showing strain. Routing tables were becoming too large to manage, the 32-bit IP address space was running low in certain classes, and the informal security model was no longer adequate for commercial use.

The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) convened to identify the most urgent problems. They reached consensus on four basic assumptions about the next 5 to 10 years: TCP/IP and OSI would coexist, the Internet would always contain diverse networks, commercial networks would be mixed with public ones, and the architecture must scale to 10^9 networks or more.
sections.eli5: The Internet was getting too big for its original design. Network leaders met and agreed on what would happen next: many different networks would join together, business networks would mix with research ones, and the system had to grow to serve way more users and computers.

sections.title: Routing and Addressing Redesign
sections.content:
The most urgent architectural problem was routing and addressing. IP addresses were assigned in fixed classes (A, B, C); class B addresses were already running out, and the entire 32-bit address space would eventually exhaust. The number of individual network numbers was also growing to the point where routers could not store routes to all of them.

The recommended approach was address aggregation: instead of routing to individual networks, group them into larger administrative domains and route to those domains. This would reduce routing table size dramatically. Three possible address formats were considered: reusing 32-bit addresses with local scope (with gateway translation), expanding to 64-bit addresses, or using 64 bits as a flat host identifier with connection setup. The document emphasized that migration to a new addressing system would take many years and must be planned comprehensively, not in incremental small changes.
sections.eli5: The number addresses each computer could have was running out. The answer was to group computers into regions and route messages to the regions instead of to each computer individually. This would let the Internet keep growing for decades.

sections.title: Supporting Multiple Protocol Suites
sections.content:
The Internet faced a fundamental architectural question: how to support both TCP/IP and the emerging OSI protocol suite simultaneously. The document proposed a process-based model with four parts. The first is the core Internet architecture built on TCP/IP, which remains the magnetic center of the Internet even as it expands.

The second and third parts represent expansion mechanisms: link sharing (where TCP/IP and OSI share physical resources without interacting, called 'ships in the night') and application interoperability (where application relays allow systems using different protocols to exchange data). The fourth part, hybridization and integration, recognizes that the Internet naturally tends to move back toward uniform, compatible protocols. Examples include running X.400 mail over RFC 1006 on TCP/IP, and developing protocol hybrids like Integrated IS-IS.
sections.eli5: Different computers wanted to use different languages to talk to each other. The answer was to let them coexist by sharing the same wires, then gradually merge the best parts of each language into hybrid versions everyone could use.

sections.title: Building Security into the Architecture
sections.content:
The original Internet was designed for military and research use with minimal security. As the Internet expanded commercially, security became essential but difficult to retrofit. The document identified five key principles: simplicity (to be understood and implemented correctly), testability, trust requirements, appropriate technology, and clear security perimeter identification.

Four possible security perimeters were identified: link-level (encryption on each wire), network/subnet-level (security at gateway routers), host-level (external security at the network interface), and process/application-level (like Privacy Enhanced Mail). The document called for an Internet-wide security architecture, including distinguished names, public key infrastructure, certificates, and cryptographic algorithms (DES, RSA, MD5). It specifically recommended developing the X.500 directory service to support this infrastructure and implementing Privacy Enhanced Mail as a concrete step.
sections.eli5: The Internet wasn't designed with security in mind. To fix this, architects proposed adding cryptographic locks at different levels and creating a global name service so people and servers could be identified and trusted.

sections.title: Supporting Real-Time Applications
sections.content:
The original Internet provided only best-effort delivery: every packet received equal treatment, with no guarantees. This was fine for email and file transfer, but voice and video required reliable, timely delivery within bounded delays. The document called for routers to implement traffic control mechanisms and per-connection state, allowing some packets to be prioritized and resources to be reserved.

Key technical challenges included deciding how to set up resource reservations (hard state like in circuit switching or soft state that times out), whether to combine resource reservation with routing protocols, and how to handle multicast delivery. The document emphasized that this would require a long-term research effort and coordination with the proposed DARTnet testbed, and that the forwarding path in routers would need to be redesigned to support these new features.
sections.eli5: Voice and video need a promise that messages arrive quickly and in order. The Internet needed to change routers so they could reserve space and priority for important traffic.
